active_themes.label: Warsh's Hawkish Hold
active_themes.summary: Warsh held rates steady today but explicitly signaled hikes are on the table before year-end. This directly contradicts the soft-landing narrative that carried equities higher through May. Equities have not repriced into this signal because Iran oil relief dominated the two-day news cycle. The critical question: will lenders move first to compress margins, or will another Fed official's public warning force equities to recalibrate before that happens?

active_themes.label: Oil Relief Window Closing
active_themes.summary: Oil collapsed below $80 on an Iran deal framework announcement, but deal details remain vague—sanctions relief terms and nuclear verification are unresolved. Markets treated this as inflation relief when the real inflation (4.2% core, sticky wages) is decoupled from energy. Oil will retest $82+ within days as talks stall or Iran escalates. The repricing trigger is not geopolitical—it's lender action.

active_themes.label: Lenders Waiting—Margin Compression Next
active_themes.summary: Discover, Capital One, and American Express had cover today to announce deposit rate cuts or tighten credit standards. All stayed silent. They are deliberately waiting for geopolitical euphoria to fade before moving. Within 3-7 days, when oil stabilizes above $82, lenders will break silence. That announcement cascades directly into equity repricing.

active_themes.label: Soft Landing Dead—Lender Action Pending
active_themes.summary: Today's 1.21% equity decline (masked by oil relief and Greenspan's death coverage) proves equities have not repriced into stagflation. Warsh's explicit hike signal + zero spending growth in May + 4.2% sticky inflation = Fed will cut into demand destruction. Equities are wrong by 8-12% based on historical stagflation scenarios. The repricing depends entirely on lender action, not geopolitical headlines.

active_themes.label: Bonds Pricing Stagflation Correctly
active_themes.summary: The 10-year remained flat at 3.9-4.1% despite Iran relief and Warsh's hawkish hold. Bonds are pricing the scenario accurately: Fed cuts or holds higher for longer into inflation that remains sticky because demand won't collapse fast enough. Equities rallied on temporary oil relief; bonds understood the policy signal. Yields will not move lower without hard evidence of demand destruction via credit tightening.

active_themes.label: Bonds Understand—Equities Don't
active_themes.summary: The 10-year Treasury remained flat at 3.9-4.1% despite Iran oil relief and Warsh's hawkish hold. Bonds understand the scenario correctly: the Fed will hike (or hold higher for longer) into stagflation. Equities rallied on oil relief and missed the policy signal entirely. Yields will not move lower without hard evidence of demand destruction, which credit tightening will provide. This divergence confirms equities are wrong by 8-12% based on historical stagflation scenarios.

active_themes.label: Lender Silence—Timing the Announcement
active_themes.summary: Today's geopolitical relief gave lenders the cover they needed to delay announcing margin pressure. They will break that silence within 3-7 days when Iran euphoria fades and oil stabilizes back above $82. That announcement (deposit rate cuts or credit tightening) is the trigger that reprices equities from the 1.21% loss they should have taken today into the 8-12% repricing the stagflation scenario demands.

active_themes.label: Soft Landing Dead
active_themes.summary: Today's rally proves equities have not repriced into stagflation—they rallied on a temporary oil relief story instead of repricing into demand destruction. This is the last repricing window before lenders force the issue. May's 0% spending growth + 4.2% inflation + today's rally + Warsh's policy error = equities are wrong, and will correct when credit tightens, not when oil rises again.

active_themes.label: Warsh Chose Credibility Over Politics
active_themes.summary: The new Fed chair rejected the assumption that he would cut or hold silently. He explicitly signaled hikes before year-end, telegraphing that he understands 4.2% inflation cannot be cut away without demand destruction. This is a credibility play—Warsh is signaling he will not be a political Fed. The market has not yet priced the implications of a hawkish Fed in a 0% spending growth environment.
